c.v: When someone dies in Dearborn because another person or company was careless, Michigan’s Wrongful Death Act (MCL 600.2922) gives the family a claim. It does not give it in the way most families expect. The claim belongs to the estate, not to the spouse or children directly. It must be brought by a personal representative appointed by the Wayne County Probate Court. The recovery is divided among family members by a judge, not by the family. And the deadline depends on what caused the death: a crash on Michigan Avenue or I-94, a truck at the Rouge, a fall, a hospital error, a nursing home. This page explains how the process works for a Dearborn family and what to do in the first weeks.

sections.heading: How a Dearborn wrongful death claim works

c.v: Only the personal representative can bring the claim (MCL 600.2922(2)). If there is a will naming an executor, that person petitions the Wayne County Probate Court, in the Coleman A. Young Municipal Center in Detroit, for appointment; if not, a family member, usually the spouse or an adult child, petitions under Michigan’s priority rules (MCL 700.3203). The court issues letters of authority, and the personal representative then has standing to hire a lawyer for the estate and file. We file the petition as the first legal step.

Within 30 days after filing suit, the personal representative must notify in writing every person who may share: the spouse, children, descendants, parents, grandparents, brothers and sisters, the children of the deceased’s spouse, and anyone named in the will (MCL 600.2922(3), (4)).

The suit is the injury claim the person would have had, brought by the estate against whoever caused the death, in the Third Judicial Circuit Court for most defendants, the Court of Claims for the State, and the Eastern District of Michigan for federal claims. The added evidence is the death itself: the Wayne County Medical Examiner’s report, the death certificate, the Dearborn Fire Department EMS run sheet, the Corewell Health Dearborn or Detroit hospital record, and the police or fire investigation.

After a settlement or verdict, the personal representative proposes a division among the eligible family members, with notice to each; if they agree, the court approves it, and if not, the court decides based on each person’s relationship and loss (MCL 600.2922(6)). Fees and costs are approved at the same hearing. Because a judge divides the money, no family member should sign anything with an insurer; a settlement with one relative is not a settlement of the estate’s claim.

faqs.question: Who can file a wrongful death lawsuit in Dearborn?

answer.v: Only the personal representative of the estate, appointed by the Wayne County Probate Court. A spouse, child, or parent can be appointed, but must be, before the claim can be filed.
The spouse, children, descendants, parents, grandparents, siblings, stepchildren, and anyone named in the will may share. The probate court approves the division after notice to each of them.

Three years from the death for most claims, two years with a 182-day notice for medical malpractice, one year to claim no-fault survivor’s loss benefits, 120 days to notify the City or the County, and 120 days from hiring a lawyer to notify a bar. The savings provision can extend the deadline for an estate in limited circumstances, but should not be relied on.

faqs.question: We buried our family member within a day. Does that affect the case?

answer.v: Not the claim itself. The Medical Examiner’s findings, the hospital and EMS records, and the police investigation establish the cause of death. Where an autopsy was not performed, the medical record and the circumstances carry the case.

faqs.question: My family member died at work at the Rouge. Is that a wrongful death case?

answer.v: The employer owes workers’ compensation death benefits and cannot otherwise be sued, but any contractor, vendor, property owner, or manufacturer whose negligence caused the death can be, and that suit is the wrongful death claim.

faqs.question: Does the family pay anything up front?

answer.v: No. The case is handled on contingency, costs are advanced by the firm, and the fee and costs are approved by the probate court at the distribution hearing.
